claims.text: A well-engineered dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure enhances creep resistance.
Nanoscale FCC regions interwoven with a BCC matrix create concentrated interphase boundaries.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries impede dislocation glide and climb and thereby delay progressive plastic deformation.
FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coatings can be deposited by methods such as HVOF or laser cladding.
The starting coating has distributed FCC regions embedded in a BCC matrix.
A coating with abundant coherent FCC/BCC boundaries can be compared with a nearly single-phase FCC or BCC coating to isolate the effect of the dual-phase structure.
Elevated temperature and moderate-to-high constant stress promote creep deformation under continuous loading.
Rapid solidification or controlled thermal treatment can produce the proposed FCC/BCC boundary network and associated nanoscale precipitates or lamellae.
During sustained high-temperature loading, dislocations generated in relatively soft FCC regions attempt to glide.
Slip-system incompatibility across FCC/BCC interfaces impedes dislocation propagation.
Lattice distortion inherent to the high-entropy alloy further impedes dislocation propagation.
Interface barriers cause dislocation pile-up or redirection and require greater stress for continued plastic flow.
The proposed interface-barrier mechanism reduces the overall creep strain rate.
Under identical creep conditions, the dual-phase coating will have a lower steady-state creep strain rate than the nearly single-phase control.
Under identical creep conditions, the dual-phase coating will have a higher creep stress exponent than the nearly single-phase control.
A nearly homogeneous FCC- or BCC-dominant coating exhibits more pronounced progressive plastic deformation during constant-load creep testing.
At elevated temperature, dislocation glide and climb remain active while interphase boundaries become important to creep resistance.
Outside the relevant stress and temperature ranges, the phase-boundary barrier effect may cease to dominate deformation.
The quantitative creep response depends on phase ratio, interface coherency, and grain-size distribution.
Processing and environmental oxidation may alter the coating response by changing its phase composition and properties.
